name: Lena Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fenwick's, a three-bay garage on the high street of a market town, about forty minutes from the nearest city. I'm one of two people there qualified to do the yearly roadworthiness test, the safety inspection every car over three years old needs, so a lot of my morning is that. Afternoons it's whatever comes in: farmers' pickups, a school minibus, a quad bike with a mangled axle. I like knowing half the cars by sight; what wears me out is the paperwork for the tests, which seems to grow every year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else is at Fenwick's, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Gordon owns it, his wife Jean does the books and the phone, and there's Aled, an apprentice who's keen but chatty. I live on my own in a rented terrace and I'm saving for a deposit on a little house, about four months' worth of money so far. I use an AI app now and then, mostly to check recall notices or to word an awkward quote. I'm not anti-technology; I just like to see it work before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overblown, and that the useful bits, like checking recall lists, were worth having. At work I'd tell Gordon he can stop worrying about it. I wouldn't post anything; I'm not really an online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's fine for me. A small garage in a town where everyone knows you has steady work, and the tests have to be done every year by law. My only real stress is house prices running ahead of my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep putting 300 a month into the deposit. I might do the extra qualification to test vans and light lorries, because the farmers would use it. Otherwise, no changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really, apart from the house thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the house thing look like, in numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The little terraces on Mill Lane go for about 150,000 now, so I need ten per cent, so fifteen thousand plus fees. I've got about seven. At 300 a month that's two and a half years if prices sit still, which they won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the van testing qualification change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Gordon said he'd pay me more if I could test the farm vans, maybe a couple of thousand a year. That shaves a few months off the deposit.

say: I'd say AI was **overblown**, though the recall checks were useful.
I'd tell Gordon he can **stop worrying**, but wouldn't post anything.
think: A small-town garage with **legally required tests** has steady work.
My only real stress is **house prices** running ahead of my savings.
do: Keep putting **300 a month** into the house deposit.
Take the **van testing qualification** to inspect farmers' vans and light lorries.
feel: **Calm and settled**, apart from worrying about buying a house.
S0.quote: A small garage in a town where everyone knows you has steady work, and the tests have to be done every year by law.
fieldNote: Security rests on **local trust** and the legal inspection requirement.
Her stress is **housing**, with a precise deposit gap of about eight thousand.
Plans a **skills upgrade** for pay, not for fear of AI.

steps.text: Save 300 a month toward a house on Mill Lane
Qualify to test vans and light lorries for local farmers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should take it seriously but not panic. I'd say the trick is to learn the useful tools and keep the skills people still need. That's what I'd tell Aled, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my hands-on work is fine for a while. The test paperwork, the quotes and the booking are a third of my day, and AI does that easily. Jean's job on the phone and the books goes first, which would be awful for her. Gordon might decide he doesn't need two testers if the computer does half the inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new testing software properly as soon as it came in, and offer to run the AI booking system so Jean isn't on her own with it. I'd keep saving but maybe slow the house plan for a year to see where things settle. And I'd get the van qualification so I'm the tester Gordon keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled. It's on my mind, but I don't feel in danger yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gordon might not need two testers. Who's the other one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon himself, actually, and he's sixty. So really I think he'd stop testing and keep me, but I'd want to make sure. Being the one who knows the new system helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Slowing the house plan, what would that mean day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving the same, I just wouldn't sign a mortgage until I saw how the garage was doing. Another year in the rented terrace isn't the end of the world. The landlord's fine and the boiler works, mostly.

say: I'd say take it **seriously but don't panic**.
I'd tell Aled to **learn the tools** and keep skills people still need.
think: Test paperwork, quotes and booking are **a third** of my day, and AI does them easily.
**Jean's job** on the phone and books goes first, and Gordon may need fewer testers.
do: Learn the **new testing software** as soon as it arrives.
Offer to run the **AI booking system** alongside Jean.
Delay signing a **mortgage** for a year while still saving.
feel: **A bit unsettled**, but not in danger yet.
S1.quote: The test paperwork, the quotes and the booking are a third of my day, and AI does that easily.
fieldNote: She estimates the **thinking share** of her job at about a third.
Worry centres on **Jean**, the owner's wife, rather than herself.
Plans to be **the indispensable tester** by mastering the new system.

steps.text: Learn the new inspection software as soon as Fenwick's installs it
Help Jean run the AI booking system at the garage
Hold off signing a mortgage for a year while saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and nobody's in charge, which is worrying. I'd want the government to pause the robots side until people can catch up. I'd say it quietly, though; I'm not a shouter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 the inspection is a sensor and a computer, and the paperwork vanishes. Then by 2031 a robot does the brake pads too. Out here it might take a bit longer to reach Fenwick's, but I'd be thirty when AGI comes and thirty-one when the robots start, and I've nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plan and keep the money as a cushion, because a mortgage with no job is the worst thing I can think of. I'd look at retraining for something with people in it, maybe the ambulance service or the fire service, which still need hands and nerve. In the first year I'd keep working at Fenwick's and apply in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit sick, but I'd still feel like I had choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the ambulance or fire service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because those are jobs where you need a person turning up, calm, on a bad day. I've done first aid at work for years and I'm good in a crisis. And they'll need people who can cut open a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents not to panic, that I've got savings and I'll find something. My dad would offer me the spare room, and I'd probably say no and then end up taking it.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and nobody's in charge.
I'd call quietly for a **pause on robots** until people catch up.
think: By 2028 the inspection is a **sensor and a computer**.
By 2031 robots do **brake pads too**, and I've nothing else to fall back on.
do: Stop the **house plan** and keep the deposit as a cushion.
Apply in the evenings for **ambulance or fire service** work.
Keep working at **Fenwick's** during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit sick, but still feels she has choices.
S2.quote: A mortgage with no job is the worst thing I can think of.
fieldNote: Sees the **inspection itself** as thinking work that AGI absorbs in 2028.
Turns to **crisis jobs** where calm presence and car-cutting skills matter.
Has **parents nearby** as a fallback, though she resists using it.

steps.text: Stop the house purchase and keep the deposit as a cushion
Apply to the ambulance or fire service in the evenings
Keep working at Fenwick's during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but enough, if people are sensible about it. I'd tell Aled to pick his trade carefully. I'd say the government should help small garages through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still my whole trade going, just later. AGI by 2031 takes the inspection and the paperwork, and I'd still have the hands-on until about 2034. Seven years is enough to change careers once, properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably buy a smaller house than I'd planned, a one-bed flat maybe, so the mortgage is small. Then I'd start the fire service application within two years, while I'm still young enough for the fitness test. I'd keep the testing job until I was in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like nervous before a driving test. There's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the fitness test. Is that a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'm fit from the job, but they want you running and lifting under pressure. I'd start training with the running club on Tuesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy at all, if the job is going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because renting forever out here means paying someone else's mortgage. A small flat I could cover on a lower wage. That's the sensible middle.

say: I'd say five years is **short but enough**, if people are sensible.
I'd say the **government** should help small garages through it.
think: It's still my **whole trade** going, just later.
Seven years until robots is **enough to change careers** once, properly.
do: Buy a **one-bed flat** with a small mortgage instead of a house.
Apply to the **fire service** within two years.
Train with the **running club** on Tuesdays for the fitness test.
feel: **Nervous**, like before a driving test, but with a plan.
S3.quote: Seven years is enough to change careers once, properly.
fieldNote: Counts **seven years** using the 2034 robot date.
A **middle path**: buys smaller rather than not at all.
Worries about the **fitness test**, and starts training now.

steps.text: Buy a one-bed flat with a small mortgage
Apply to the fire service within two years
Run with the local club on Tuesdays to pass the fitness test

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time for most people to sort themselves out, as long as there's help. I'd tell people not to throw away a good trade too early. Fenwick's will need someone for a while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty with the robots. Plenty of time to buy the house, pay a chunk off, and decide. It's a worry for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house on Mill Lane as planned in two or three years. I'd keep learning the testing software as it changes. Around thirty-two or thirty-three I'd sit down and decide whether to switch to the fire service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide at thirty-two rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fire service has age and fitness limits, more or less, and I wouldn't want to start at forty. So I'd decide in my early thirties. That gives me time to see how AI is actually doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Gordon and Fenwick's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon will have retired by then, I'd guess. Maybe I'd buy into the garage, if it's still worth anything. That's the other option.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time**, as long as there's help.
I'd tell people not to **throw away** a good trade too early.
think: Forty when robots come gives me **plenty of time**.
I can buy the house, **pay a chunk off**, and then decide.
do: Buy the **Mill Lane house** in two or three years as planned.
Keep learning the **testing software** as it changes.
Decide around **thirty-two** whether to join the fire service.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, but mostly fine.
S4.quote: Fenwick's will need someone for a while yet.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **keep the house plan**.
Sets a **decision point** in her early thirties because of fire service age limits.
Considers **buying into the garage** when Gordon retires.

steps.text: Buy the house on Mill Lane in two or three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd starve, but because I'd have no time to make a sensible choice, and I like sensible choices. What would help is help for small garages to adapt, and a fast route into jobs like the fire service for people who already have practical skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about places like ours, out of the city. Everyone assumes the robots come everywhere at once. Out here the robots will come last, but so will the help.

headlineQuote: Out here the robots will come last, but so will the help.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old mechanic** and inspection tester at a small market-town garage.
She lives alone, renting, and is **saving for a house** on Mill Lane.
Pragmatic and steady, she uses AI **now and then** and trusts what's proven.
She shifts from **calm to anxious** as AGI nears, planning a move to the fire service.
Every scenario is filtered through **the house decision** and keeping sensible choices open.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to make a sensible career choice.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small garages** to adapt to new tools.
A **fast route** into the fire service for people with practical skills.
